awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Evaluating compensatory socialization mechanisms and physiological responses to conspecific loss
awd_abstract_narration:
Social loss, or the death of a member of the group, is usually a stressful experience for partners, to which humans respond by increasing social efforts that strengthen social bonds. These responses are compensatory socialization mechanisms that attenuate stress, thus mitigating the negative effects of loss. This dissertation research project provides broader comparative and evolutionary context to advance our understanding of responses to social loss.  The PI assesses the behavioral and physiological responses that follow the loss of social partners in a social non-human primate species, evaluating whether social loss leads to long term consequences and comparing the physiological and behavioral responses of the study species with those observed in humans.  The study provides research, mentoring, and educational opportunities to students and the general public. 

This study assesses how the loss of individuals from a community may differentially affect surviving bond and non-bond partners in a wild non-human primate species. To this end, the study integrates historic, behavioral, and physiological data. Longitudinal and newly collected social data are used to map social networks. Behavioral data is evaluated to determine whether compensatory socialization mechanisms follow conspecific loss in this species. Ultimately, analyses address how individuals that live in fission-fusion groups behaviorally compensate for the death of a social partner, and how loss affects their social networks. The longitudinal analyses assess whether loss has a long-term impact on health and well being.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Loss is a regular and painful part of the human condition. From family deaths to breakups, moving schools as a teenager to leaving a job as an adult, our species is acutely aware of how disturbances to our social network can alter our psychological state, physiology, and long-term quality of life. In humans, social support buffers individuals from anxiety and depression, increases life expectancy and reproductive success — among other benefits to general well-being and fitness. Conversely, social isolation and lack of support can have just as, if not more, pronounced effects on mortality than chronic disease. This project aims to contribute to our understanding of parallel patterns and processes observed, often anecdotally, in other social mammals. To that end, we asses behavioral and physiological responses to the loss and absence of bond partners in a social non-human primate species, chimpanzees.

Two field seasons have been completed in service to collecting behavioral and noninvasive physiological data for this project. We collected and completed onsite analysis of cortisol from urine samples for hundreds of samples and are completing data entry for paired behavioral data to assess the response of focal chimpanzee cortisol levels to the presence or absence of close social partners. 

Intellectual Merit

Pilot data for this project has supported the development of our understanding of how social mammals cope with loss. We found that after the death of stronger partners, female chimpanzees at at Gombe National Park moved away from areas they previously shared with a friend. For adult females, the loss of a mother or a daughter also came with the loss of habitat quality. Data collected in the field will be integrated into broader analytical plans to further characterize social and physiological response to death.

Broader Impacts

This project has carried out public education and outreach throughout the duration of the award period, including training and of undergraduate students in data analysis and coding, advising of undergraduate students for honors thesis work, training undergraduate American and Tanzanian Laboratory Staff in enzyme linked immunoassay procedure, analysis, and interpretation. CO-PI McClain has delivered public outreach talks at the Smithsonian Museum of Natural History and continued collaborating with primary school level outreach through the Letters to a Prescientist program.

The scope of the work for the project has been completed, and we do not anticipate any further action on the award.
